title: Real-life phrases with rise and fall
purpose: Explore rise and fall in phrases you actually use, and find a style that feels like you.
instructions: Make a list of short phrases you say often in real life.
Try more rise and fall in your voice, so it sounds more animated.
Stress the words that carry the meaning.
Then try longer phrases you would really say.
Record yourself and listen back to decide what feels like you.

primary_cue.text: Let the rise and fall follow what you mean.

cues.text: Let the rise and fall follow what you mean.
Try a little more rise and fall, then listen back.
Stress only the words that carry the meaning.

practice_task.prompt_text: When do you want dinner? What are you up to today?

check_questions.text: Did the rise and fall fit the meaning and feel like you?

expected_observations: Changing intonation involves small changes in volume, pitch, speech rate and facial expression.
common_misunderstandings: You don't need an exaggerated melody, a particular accent or particular words. The source suggests exaggerating may help while exploring; in Lilt that is optional.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
adaptations: Replace the example phrases with your own.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt does not judge whether your intonation is right. A falling pitch at the end of a sentence is not automatically wrong.
